entry: American actor and military officer. Known for his distinctive drawl and everyman screen persona, Stewart appeared in 80 films from 1935 to 1991. He won the Academy Award for Best Actor for *The Philadelphia Story* (1940) and starred in [[Frank Capra]]'s *Mr. Smith Goes to Washington* (1939) and *It's a Wonderful Life* (1946). He starred in four films directed by [[Alfred Hitchcock]], including *Rope* (1948), *Rear Window* (1954) and *Vertigo* (1958). He began acting while at [[Princeton University]]. During [[World War II]] he enlisted in the U.S. Army Air Forces and rose to deputy commanding officer of the 2nd Bombardment Wing. He retired in 1968 as a brigadier general.

American singer-songwriter and guitarist. After breaking through with the No. 3 hit "Fire and Rain", Taylor had his first No. 1 hit in 1971 with "You've Got a Friend", written by [[Carole King]]. His 1976 album *Greatest Hits* sold 11 million copies in the U.S. alone. He won six Grammy Awards and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2000. He starred in the 1971 film *Two-Lane Blacktop*.

King of Scotland (1567–1625) and of England and Ireland (1603–1625). The son of [[Mary, Queen of Scots]] and Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley, James acceded to the Scottish throne at the age of thirteen months, after his mother was forced to abdicate. He succeeded his cousin Elizabeth I in 1603, uniting the crowns of Scotland and England in his person, though the two kingdoms kept separate parliaments and laws. He long sought a closer political union without success. His reign included the [[Gunpowder Plot]] of 1605 and conflicts with the English Parliament. He sponsored the translation later known as the [[King James Version|Authorized King James Version]] of the Bible and wrote *Daemonologie* (1597). He tried to avoid involvement in the [[Thirty Years' War]]. His reign in Scotland was the longest of any Scottish monarch. He was succeeded by his second son, Charles I.

Malaysian-born Australian filmmaker. Wan is best known for horror films, including the *Saw* and *Insidious* franchises and The Conjuring Universe, the highest-grossing horror franchise at over $2.9 billion. He directed the first *Saw* film in 2004. He also directed *Furious 7* (2015) and *Aquaman* (2018), and he founded the production company Atomic Monster. His films have grossed over $4.1 billion worldwide.

American molecular biologist, geneticist and zoologist. In 1953 Watson and [[Francis Crick]] proposed the double helix structure of [[DNA]] in a paper published in *Nature*, which built on research by [[Rosalind Franklin]] and Raymond Gosling. In 1962 Watson, Crick and Maurice Wilkins shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries concerning the molecular structure of [[nucleic acid|nucleic acids]]. Watson taught at [[Harvard University]] from 1956 to 1976 and directed Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory from 1968, where he shifted research toward cancer. His book *The Double Helix* (1968) became a bestseller. His later remarks linking genes to race and intelligence led to his resignation as chancellor of the laboratory in 2007 and to the revocation of his honorary titles in 2019.

Scottish inventor, engineer and chemist. While working as an instrument maker at the University of Glasgow, Watt improved the [[steam engine|steam engine]] of Thomas Newcomen. Newcomen's design repeatedly cooled and reheated the cylinder, wasting energy. Watt's separate condenser avoided this waste and greatly improved the power and efficiency of steam engines. He adapted the engine to produce rotary motion, broadening its use beyond pumping water, and his steam engine of 1776 was fundamental to the [[Industrial Revolution]]. In 1775 he formed a partnership with Matthew Boulton, and the firm of Boulton and Watt became highly successful. As Watt developed the concept of [[Horsepower|horsepower]], the SI unit of power, the [[Watt|watt]], was named after him.

Infrared space telescope launched in 2021. Designed for infrared astronomy, it is the largest telescope in space and can view objects too old, distant or faint for the [[Hubble Space Telescope]]. Its primary mirror has 18 hexagonal segments made of gold-plated beryllium, and the telescope must be kept below 50 K. It launched from French Guiana on December 25, 2021, and reached an orbit near the Sun–Earth L2 [[Lagrange point]] in January 2022. NASA led the project with the [[European Space Agency]] and the Canadian Space Agency, and [[Northrop Grumman]] was the primary contractor. It is named after James E. Webb, NASA administrator from 1961 to 1968.

English settlement in the Colony of Virginia, founded in 1607. Established by the Virginia Company of London as James Fort, it was the first permanent English settlement in the [[Americas]]. Earlier English attempts, including the [[Roanoke Colony]], had failed. Only 60 of the original 214 settlers survived the 1609–1610 winter known as the Starving Time. In 1612 West Indies [[Tobacco|tobacco]] was successfully cultivated, bringing an economic boom. The year 1619 saw the first legislative assembly in the New World. Jamestown was the colonial capital until 1699, when the capital moved to present-day Williamsburg. Today it survives as an archaeological site.

Persian poet, scholar and Sufi mystic. Jami is known for his mystical Sufi literature and his analysis of the metaphysics of mercy. His family moved to [[Herat]] when he was young, and while there he held an important position at the [[Timurid Empire|Timurid court]]. He completed his studies in [[Samarkand]]. He belonged to the Naqshbandi order of [[Sufism]] and was a Sunni. His most famous poetic works include *Haft Awrang*, *Tuhfat al-Ahrar* and *Layla wa Majnun*. He was a mentor and friend of the Turkic poet Alisher Navoi.

American banker and manager. Dimon has been chief executive of [[JPMorgan Chase]] since 2005 and its chairman since 2006. After graduating from Harvard Business School in 1982, he joined American Express under Sandy Weill. He became president of Citigroup in 1998. In 2000 he became chief executive of Bank One, which merged with JPMorgan Chase in 2004. He served on the board of the [[Federal Reserve]] Bank of New York in the late 2010s. *Time* magazine included him in its 2006, 2008, 2009 and 2011 lists of the world's 100 most influential people.

American comedian, actor and singer. Foxx gained his breakthrough as a featured player on the sketch comedy show *In Living Color* from 1991 to 1994. He then starred in the [[Sitcom|sitcom]] *The Jamie Foxx Show*. He won the Academy Award for Best Actor for portraying [[Ray Charles]] in *Ray* (2004). He had two Billboard Hot 100 number-one singles as a featured artist, "Slow Jamz" by Twista with [[Kanye West]] and "Gold Digger" by West. Since 2017 he has hosted the Fox game show *Beat Shazam*.

American actress, producer and children's author. Known for horror and slasher films, she is regarded as a "scream queen". She starred as Laurie Strode in John Carpenter's *Halloween* (1978) and in six Halloween sequels. Her comedies include *Trading Places* (1983) and *Everything Everywhere All at Once* (2022), which won her an Academy Award. She is the daughter of actors [[Tony Curtis]] and [[Janet Leigh]]. Her children's books have made [[The New York Times]] best-seller list.

English celebrity chef and restaurateur. Oliver rose to prominence with the [[BBC]] Two series *The Naked Chef* (1999–2001), known for its casual approach to cuisine. In 2005 he began the Feed Me Better campaign to bring healthier food to schoolchildren, which the government later backed. His restaurant chain, Jamie's Italian, opened in 2008 and went into administration in 2019. As an author, Oliver had sold more than 50.6 million books. He was appointed a Member of the Order of the British Empire in 2003.

Union territory administered by India, forming the southern portion of the larger [[Kashmir]] region. It has been the subject of a border dispute between India and Pakistan since 1947 and between India and China since 1959. In 2019 the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganization Act reconstituted the former state as two union territories, with Ladakh separated to the east. [[Srinagar]] and Jammu jointly serve as the capital. The region has deposits of [[Sapphire|sapphire]], borax and [[Graphite|graphite]]. [[Horticulture|Horticulture]], handicrafts and tourism are important to the economy, and apple cultivation employs 3.5 million people.

Indian industrialist and philanthropist. Tata founded a trading company in 1868 at the age of 29. He established Empress Mill in [[Nagpur]] and converted a bankrupt oil mill in [[Mumbai]] into a cotton mill. He founded the Taj Mahal Hotel in Mumbai, India's first hotel with electricity, and helped establish Tata Steel and Tata Power. He also founded the [[Tata Group]], which he led as patriarch of the Tata family, and he established the city of Jamshedpur. [[Jawaharlal Nehru]] called him a "One-Man Planning Commission". His philanthropy focused on education and healthcare.

Czech theologian, philosopher and church reformer. Hus preached in [[Prague]] and opposed many practices of the Catholic Church in Bohemia, including simony and the sale of indulgences. He is considered the first church reformer, although some designate [[John Wycliffe]] as the first. Excommunicated by papal bull, he was arrested at the Council of Constance, refused to recant and was burned at the stake for heresy on July 6, 1415. His followers, the Hussites, defeated five consecutive papal crusades between 1420 and 1431 in the [[Hussite Wars]]. His teachings influenced [[Protestantism]] and, over a century later, [[Martin Luther]].

Czech military commander and Hussite leader. A follower of [[Jan Hus]], Žižka led the Taborite faction of the [[Hussite Wars]] and is celebrated as a Czech national hero. He led Hussite forces against three [[Crusades|crusades]] and is said to have remained undefeated. He won battles at Sudoměř and Vítkov Hill in 1420 and defeated the army of the [[Holy Roman Empire]] and the Hungarian Kingdom at Kutná Hora in 1421. He used armored wagon forts fitted with small cannons, anticipating the [[Tank|tank]] of later centuries. A monument on Vítkov Hill in [[Prague]] honors him; it is the third-largest bronze equestrian statue in the world.

Early Netherlandish painter. Van Eyck was one of the leading innovators of early Netherlandish painting and one of the supreme figures of the Early Northern Renaissance. He was court painter to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, and was sent on diplomatic missions, including one to [[Lisbon]] in 1428. Vasari called him the inventor of [[Oil painting|oil painting]], a claim now considered an oversimplification. About 20 surviving paintings are confidently attributed to him, including the Ghent Altarpiece, and his works include altarpieces, triptychs and [[Portrait|portraits]]. His early work moved beyond the International Gothic style toward naturalism and realism.

American settlement activist and reformer. In 1889 Addams co-founded Hull House in [[Chicago]], one of America's most famous settlement houses, providing social services to poor, largely immigrant families. She was a leader in the history of [[Social work|social work]] and [[Women's suffrage|women's suffrage]]. An advocate for [[World peace]], she shared the 1931 Nobel Peace Prize with Nicholas Murray Butler, becoming the first American woman to receive it. In 1920 she co-founded the American Civil Liberties Union. She was one of the most prominent reformers of the [[Progressive Era]].

English novelist. Her six novels implicitly interpret, critique and comment on the English landed gentry at the end of the 18th century. Her plots often explore women's dependence on marriage for social standing and economic security. She wrote major novels before the age of 22 but was not published until she was 35. *Sense and Sensibility* (1811), *Pride and Prejudice* (1813), *Mansfield Park* (1814) and *Emma* (1815) were published anonymously with moderate success. *Northanger Abbey* and *Persuasion* appeared posthumously, and *Sanditon* was left unfinished at her death. Her work is known for social commentary, realism, wit and irony.

Novel by English writer [[Charlotte Brontë]], published in 1847 under the pen name Currer Bell. A bildungsroman narrated in the first person, it follows an orphan from her childhood at Gateshead Hall and her education at Lowood School to her years as governess at Thornfield Hall, where she falls in love with Edward Fairfax Rochester. The novel revolutionized prose fiction by focusing on the moral and spiritual development of its heroine. It combines social criticism with Christian morality and addresses class, sexuality, religion and [[Feminism|feminism]]. Along with *Pride and Prejudice*, it is among the most famous romance novels. In 2003 the [[BBC]] ranked it tenth best-loved book in Britain in its Big Read poll.

American actress and activist. Fonda won two Academy Awards for Best Actress, for *Klute* (1971) and *Coming Home* (1978). In 1972 she visited [[Hanoi]] during the [[Vietnam War]], where she was photographed on a North Vietnamese anti-aircraft gun and gained the nickname "Hanoi Jane". Her 1982 exercise video *Jane Fonda's Workout* became the highest-selling VHS ever. She describes herself as a [[Feminism|feminist]] and environmental activist, and she cofounded the Hollywood Women's Political Committee in 1984.

English primatologist and anthropologist. Goodall is known for more than six decades of field research on wild chimpanzees in Gombe Stream National Park, Tanzania, which began in 1960 under the mentorship of Louis Leakey. Her research showed that chimpanzees use tools, have complex emotions, form lasting social bonds and engage in organized warfare, which redefined the traditional view that humans are uniquely different from other animals. She earned a PhD in ethology from the [[University of Cambridge]] in 1965. In 1977 she founded the Jane Goodall Institute. She wrote 32 books, and her first, *In the Shadow of Man* (1971), was translated into 48 languages.

American-Canadian journalist, author and urban theorist. Her book *The Death and Life of Great American Cities* (1961) argued that urban renewal and slum clearance did not respect the needs of city dwellers. She organized opposition to Robert Moses's plans for Greenwich Village and helped end the Lower Manhattan Expressway. She was arrested in 1968 for inciting a crowd at a public hearing on that project. After moving to [[Toronto]] that year, she opposed the Spadina Expressway. Critics noted that she lacked formal training in [[Urban planning|urban planning]], but professionals such as Richard Florida acknowledged her influence on urban studies, sociology and economics.

American actress. Wyman won the Academy Award for Best Actress for *Johnny Belinda* (1948) and received four Best Actress nominations between 1946 and 1954. Her films include *The Lost Weekend* (1945), *The Yearling* (1946) and *All That Heaven Allows* (1955). She produced and hosted the final three seasons of the [[NBC]] program *Fireside Theatre*, which was rebranded with her name. Her television career was revived by the [[Soap opera|soap opera]] *Falcon Crest* (1981–1990), in which she played the villainous matriarch Angela Channing. She was the first wife of [[Ronald Reagan]].
